text:
kevin: hey all, first day and I can authenticate to the VPN but can't reach internal services. `ping intranet.redwood.internal` resolves to 10.10.1.5 but the ping goes to a device on my home LAN (shows 10.10.1.5 with my router's MAC). using the WireGuard newhire-prod profile on macOS. anyone seen address collisions like this? :grimacing:

it-ops: ohhh classic home subnet collision. does your home router actually use 10.10.1.0/24? can you paste `ifconfig` (or `ipconfig getifaddr en0`) and `netstat -rn` output?

kevin: yeah my ISP's router uses 10.10.1.0/24 for the home network (ugh). `ipconfig getifaddr en0` is 10.10.1.22. `netstat -rn` shows a route for 10.10.1.0/24 via en0 so the host never sends 10.10.1.x traffic over wg0. hitting internal services from work laptop on corporate WiFi was fine.

neteng: yup that's the symptom. When internal ranges overlap a local LAN, the kernel prefers the local route so the VPN routes never apply. a few options: 1) easiest for you: change your home router LAN to a different private range (e.g., 192.168.50.0/24) — reboot router and laptop. 2) temporary: add a more specific route for the internal subnets pointing to the wg interface so the kernel sends traffic to VPN despite local interface. on macOS:```sudo route -n add -net 10.10.0.0/16 -interface utun1```(replace utun1 with your wg device)
3) alternative: tether to phone hotspot (carrier NAT will almost always avoid RFC1918 collisions).

jamie: note — option 2 works but is fragile: if your home LAN is also 10.10.1.0/24 you might see ARP conflicts for the same IP on different segments. we'd prefer you change the home subnet if possible. If you can't access the router (renter/ISP-managed), option 2 plus using `arp -d 10.10.1.5` can occasionally help but it's hacky.

kevin: I don't have access to change ISP router settings. tried the route add command but `route` says "No such process" for that interface name. how do I find the right interface?

it-ops: run `ifconfig` and look for the WireGuard/wg interface name (it might be `utun2` or `wg0` depending on the client). example:```ifconfig | grep -B2 'inet 10.10'```or check `wg` output. then `sudo route -n add -net 10.10.0.0/16 -interface <iface>` should add it. If route tool is complaining on modern macOS, use:```sudo route -n add -net 10.10.0.0/16 -gateway 10.10.2.1```where 10.10.2.1 is your wg peer gateway (check `ifconfig <iface>` for peer address).

kevin: found utun3 as the WireGuard interface. ran `sudo route -n add -net 10.10.0.0/16 -interface utun3` and then `ping intranet.redwood.internal` now goes through VPN and resolves to 10.10.1.5 but pings to the server succeed. thanks!

neteng: glad it worked. we'll still track this in the onboarding docs: action items: a) add FAQ about home LAN collisions and recommended home subnets (192.168.0.0/16 ranges like 192.168.50.0/24), b) add guidance for persistent route commands per OS, c) add a short line recommending mobile hotspot fallback.

devex-bot: created ticket #INFR-4122 to add home-subnet collision troubleshooting and per-OS persistent route snippets to the new-hire onboarding checklist and docs.

jamie: one more note for the ticket: we should detect overlap on signup (we can ask the client to report local IPs during onboarding) and warn users if their LAN matches our internal prefixes. I'll pair with infra to draft a prompt. :+1:

kevin: leaving this here for the next new-hires: if your home Wi-Fi uses 10.10.x.x you'll likely collide with Redwood's internal range. phone hotspot or a quick route add are good temporary fixes but changing your router LAN to a 192.168.X.0/24 is the clean solution. saved my first-hour panic. :relieved:
